title: Big super has a second bite at overhauling controversial RG 97
full_text:
The corporate watchdog will start a second review of controversial rules outlining what costs superannuation funds must disclose, following intense lobbying from the industry super sector.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission will next week hold the first of a series of roundtables where fund bosses will be able to air their grievances about the rule, known as RG 97. About 80 fund chief executives and major stakeholders are expected to receive invitations to roundtables.
RG 97 initially required the upfront disclosure of costs on investments such as brokerage, settlement and clearing costs, and stamp duty, which flowed into fund performance results.
It was a long-time bugbear of industry funds which argued that it skewed investment away from unlisted housing, venture capital and private equity.
For example, stamp duty payments for unlisted infrastructure such as housing had to be disclosed in the first year, while the same costs paid by listed funds were instead incorporated into their annual investment fees. This makes it appear that listed assets perform better than their unlisted equivalents.
Chief among the agitants seeking change was industry super fund Cbus, which has been lobbying the Albanese government for years on the issue. Wayne Swan, the former Labor treasurer and one-time boss of Treasurer Jim Chalmers, is Cbus chairman and in 2024 told the Senate that RG 97 “inhibits investment”.
ASIC began a review of the rule after Chalmers’ Economic Reform Roundtable last August, and in May announced changes that would allow property stamp duty paid in one year to be smoothed over seven years to even out the cost profile.
The regulator also agreed to bring forward a broader review of the rule amid anger about the distortionary effects on investment. Consultations will run over several months and any proposed changes are not expected until mid-to-late 2027.
Property lobby wants ASIC to go further
The Property Council of Australia wants ASIC to go further and axe the disclosure of stamp-duty costs, or at least have them reclassified as an incidental or operating cost.
The lobby group argued exclusion would free up $8.7 billion of investment for new housing and create 35,000 new homes. It also said other taxes on property, such as land tax, did not have to be disclosed.
The Australian Investment Council has also argued the rule makes high-fee but higher-return investments in private equity and venture capital – critical to the start-up sector – look less attractive.
Retail fund-focused Financial Services Council and consumer group Super Consumers Australia, however, oppose a complete exemption and dispute the idea the rule has skewed investment.
Liberal senator Andrew Bragg was critical of the decision to smooth stamp duty over seven years. He has argued the move gives institutional buyers an advantage over mum-and-dad investors and people who use self-managed super funds.
Bragg has accused the government of pressuring ASIC to make the change and has referred Labor’s relationship with the industry super sector to the National Anti-Corruption Commission to investigate.
